intro: A thirteen-year-old in Iowa pins a strip of black cloth to her sleeve and is sent home from school. An eighth grader in Rockford writes a letter about first period starting too early. A man in a Florida prison writes to the Supreme Court in pencil. None of them held office. All of them changed what government could do. This unit is about the machine they used: the Constitution of the United States, the Constitution of Illinois, and the rights that both promise to you.

The first chapter takes the machine apart. You will see why the framers of 1787 split power into three branches, how each branch can block the others, and how the nation and the state of Illinois divide the work between them. You will follow a bill from a student's idea through the General Assembly to the governor's desk, and you will learn who actually decides the things that touch your day: the county, the city, and the school board.

The second chapter is about the rights that limit that machine and the people who won them. You will read the Bill of Rights amendment by amendment, watch the Constitution grow to include people it once left out, and study three court cases about students, schools and police. Then you will look at the tools you can use now: voting in Illinois, reading the news without being fooled, and standing up at a microphone. By the end, you should be able to explain how a law gets made, what a court can do about it, and what you can do about both.
bigQuestion: How does a government built to limit its own power protect your rights, and what is your part in making it work?

timeline.t: Fifty-five framers in Philadelphia write a Constitution with three branches and a Preamble that begins We the People
The states ratify the first ten amendments, the Bill of Rights
In Marbury v. Madison, the Supreme Court claims the power to strike down laws that violate the Constitution
Illinois becomes a state under its first constitution, written at Kaskaskia
Illinois is the first state to ratify the Thirteenth Amendment, abolishing slavery
The Fourteenth Amendment makes everyone born in the United States a citizen and promises equal protection
The Nineteenth Amendment bars denying the vote on account of sex; Illinois had ratified it in 1919
Brown v. Board of Education rules that segregated public schools are unconstitutional
Miranda v. Arizona requires police to warn suspects of their rights before questioning
Tinker v. Des Moines protects students' peaceful speech at school
Illinois voters approve the state's fourth constitution, the one in force today
The Twenty-Sixth Amendment lowers the voting age to eighteen

words.d: the written plan for a government and its highest law
dividing government power among the legislative, executive and judicial branches
the powers each branch has to limit or block the other branches
a president's or governor's refusal to sign a bill, which stops it unless the legislature overrides
the power of courts to strike down laws or actions that violate the Constitution
a system in which power is divided between a national government and state governments
the Illinois legislature, made of a House of 118 members and a Senate of 59
the first ten amendments to the Constitution, approved in 1791
fair legal procedures the government must follow before taking life, liberty or property
the Fourteenth Amendment's rule that government must treat people in the same situation alike
the share of eligible people who actually vote in an election
discussing disagreements respectfully, attacking ideas rather than people

test.q: Which branch of the national government makes the laws?
choices: The executive branch
The legislative branch
The judicial branch
The cabinet
test.why: Congress, the legislative branch, writes and passes laws. The president enforces them and the courts interpret them.

test.q: Why did the framers divide power into three branches?
choices: To make government act quickly
To copy the British system
So that no one person or group could rule alone
Because the states demanded three branches
test.why: The framers feared concentrated power and built a system where each branch needs the others.

test.q: What does the Preamble of the Constitution do?
choices: Lists the powers of the president
Creates the Bill of Rights
Sets the number of states
Explains the purposes of the Constitution and says power comes from the people
test.why: The Preamble begins We the People and names six goals. It grants no powers itself.

test.q: What can Congress do if the president vetoes a bill?
choices: Override the veto with a two-thirds vote of both houses
Ask the Supreme Court to sign it
Send it to the states for a vote
Nothing; the bill is dead forever
test.why: A two-thirds vote in both the House and the Senate passes a bill over the president's veto.

test.q: Which of these is a power of the state of Illinois rather than the national government?
choices: Coining money
Running public schools
Declaring war
Making treaties
test.why: Schools are a reserved power of the states. Money, war and treaties belong to the national government.

test.q: How is the Illinois Supreme Court chosen?
choices: Appointed by the president
Appointed by the governor for life
Elected by voters in five districts to ten-year terms
Chosen by the General Assembly
test.why: Illinois elects its judges. Supreme Court justices serve ten-year terms and face retention votes after that.

test.q: Which local government usually sets a school district's calendar and budget?
choices: The county sheriff
The governor
The township
The school board
test.why: Each Illinois school district has an elected board that sets the budget, hires the superintendent and sets the calendar.

test.q: Which tax provides most of the money for local schools in Illinois?
choices: The property tax
The federal income tax
The gas tax
The tax on hotel rooms
test.why: Illinois schools depend heavily on property taxes, which is why districts with valuable property can spend more per student.

test.q: Which freedoms does the First Amendment protect?
choices: The right to a lawyer and a jury
Religion, speech, the press, assembly and petition
Protection from unreasonable searches
The right to vote at eighteen
test.why: The First Amendment's five freedoms are religion, speech, press, peaceful assembly and petition.

test.q: What did the Thirteenth Amendment do?
choices: Gave women the vote
Made everyone born here a citizen
Abolished slavery
Lowered the voting age
test.why: Ratified in 1865, the Thirteenth Amendment ended slavery in the United States. Illinois ratified it first.

test.q: Why is the Fourteenth Amendment called the most powerful sentence in the Constitution?
choices: Because it created the Supreme Court
Because it is the longest amendment
Because it ended the Civil War
Because its promise of equal protection binds the states and has been used to protect many groups
test.why: Equal protection and due process, applied to the states, became the basis for ending segregation and many other rights cases.

test.q: What did Tinker v. Des Moines decide?
choices: Students keep free speech rights at school unless their speech substantially disrupts learning
Schools may search any student without reason
Students may not protest in any form at school
Police must warn suspects of their rights
test.why: The Court protected the black armbands and set the substantial disruption test for student speech.

test.q: What must police do before questioning a suspect in custody, under Miranda v. Arizona?
choices: Get a warrant from a judge
Warn the suspect of the right to remain silent and to have a lawyer
Call the suspect's family
Get the suspect's signature
test.why: The Miranda warning tells a suspect in custody that they may stay silent and have a lawyer, provided free if needed.

test.q: What is the best way to check a surprising claim you see online?
choices: See how many shares it has
Judge whether the page looks professional
Leave the page and see what other reliable sources say about it and its author
Ask a friend who agrees with you
test.why: Lateral reading, checking other reliable sources about the claim and its source, is how professional fact-checkers work.

test.q: Which of these can a student under eighteen in Illinois legally do to take part in government?
choices: Vote in a November general election at sixteen
Sign a bill into law
Serve on the Illinois Supreme Court
Speak at public comment during a school board meeting
test.why: Illinois government meetings are open to the public, and anyone, including students, may speak during public comment.

write.prompt: The framers built a government that is slow on purpose. Take a position: does the system of checks and balances and federalism protect people's rights more than it gets in the way of solving problems? Use evidence from this unit, including the path of a bill in Illinois, at least one landmark court case, and one amendment.
tips: State your claim in one clear sentence: the slowness mostly protects rights, or it mostly blocks needed change.
Use specific evidence: the veto and override, judicial review in Marbury, the Illinois budget impasse, or the decades between the Fifteenth Amendment and the Voting Rights Act.
Explain your reasoning: show how each piece of evidence connects to your claim, not just that it happened.
Answer the other side honestly: name the strongest point against your claim and say why your claim still holds.
End with what a citizen your age can do inside this system, using one example from the last chapter.
